summary: Sets out requirements for signaling protocols that work across different networks, administrative domains and technologies. Signaling here is mainly for quality of service, as with RSVP, but also covers uses such as MPLS label distribution and signaling to middleboxes. It is informational and came from the NSIS working group.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3726 is the requirement list for the Next Steps in Signaling working group. It describes signalling as a way of asking the network to set up state, such as a quality of service reservation, and then says what any protocol doing that must do: be modular, be cheap on a radio link, survive failures, protect the messages, and work when the route changes under it.

questions: what are the requirements for signaling protocols
subtitle: What a signalling protocol must do if it is to work across networks, technologies and administrative borders

tldr.problem: Signalling protocols set up and maintain state in the network, for quality of service, for label distribution and for talking to middleboxes. The ones built for one network, or one technology, do not carry across administrative and technology boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: The memo starts from eleven scenarios, defines a small model of who takes part in a signalling exchange, and then lists requirements in ten groups: architecture, flows, messaging, control information, performance, flexibility, security, mobility, interworking and operation.
tldr.outcome: The requirements are deliberately independent of any one application, so the same signalling protocol can serve resource reservation, MPLS label distribution and middlebox control. The memo states no protocol of its own and lists no problems with existing ones.

facts.label: Requirement groups
facts.value: 10, from architecture and design goals to operational requirements

facts.label: Roles in the signalling model
facts.value: NSIS Initiator, NSIS Forwarder and NSIS Responder

facts.label: Scenarios in the appendix
facts.value: Terminal and session mobility, wireless and 3G networks, QoS reservation, trunking gateways and VPNs

today: RFC 3726 is an Informational memo from April 2004 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a requirement document, not a protocol, and its own security considerations section simply points at the security requirements it lists in section 5.7.

sections.title: What This Memo Is For
sections.content:
This document is the product of the Next Steps in Signaling Working Group. It defines requirements for signalling across different network environments, and it does not list any problems of existing signalling protocols such as RSVP.

To derive requirements for signalling it is necessary first to have an idea of the scope within which they apply, so the memo lists use cases and scenarios where an NSIS protocol could be applied. The scenarios are used to help derive the requirements and to test the requirements against use cases.

The requirements listed are independent of any application, although resource reservation and quality of service related issues are used as examples within the text. Quality of service is not the only field where signalling is used in the Internet: signalling might also be used as a communication protocol to set up and maintain state in middleboxes. The document does not cover requirements in relation to some networking areas, in particular interaction with host and site multihoming, and leaves these for future analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a shopping list, not a design. The authors take real situations where signalling would be useful, work out what they have in common, and write down what any protocol has to do to serve them all.

sections.title: The Pieces of the Model
sections.content:
The memo lists the terms it uses most often. They cannot be made precise without a more complete architectural model and they are not meant to prescribe any solution.

An NSIS Entity is the function within a node that implements an NSIS protocol; in the case of path-coupled signalling it will always be on the data path. An NSIS Initiator is the entity that starts signalling to set up or manipulate network state. An NSIS Forwarder is the entity between an initiator and a responder, which may interact with local state management functions in the network and also propagates signalling further through the network. An NSIS Responder is the entity that terminates signalling and can optionally interact with applications as well.

A flow is a traffic stream, a sequence of IP packets between two end systems, for which a specific packet level treatment is provided; it can be unicast, uni- or bi-directional, or multicast, and for multicast a flow can diverge as it propagates toward the receiver. The data path is the route across the networks taken by a flow or aggregate, and the signalling path is the route taken by a signalling flow or aggregate.

Path-coupled signalling is a mode where the signalling messages follow a path tied to the data packets, so they are routed only through nodes that are in the data path. Path-decoupled signalling has independent data and signalling paths: signalling messages are routed to nodes that are not assumed to be on the data path but which are aware of it, and are always directly addressed to the neighbouring entity, so the initiator and responder may have no relation at all with the ultimate data sender or receiver.

The scope of NSIS is the interaction between the initiator, the forwarders and the responder, including a protocol to carry the information and the syntax and semantics of what is exchanged. The initiator might be in the end system or elsewhere in the network, and its distinguishing feature is that it acts on triggers coming directly or indirectly from the higher layers in the end systems; it needs to map the services they request and provides feedback information which might be used by transport layer algorithms or adaptive applications. The forwarder does not interact with higher layers, but with the initiator, the responder and possibly other forwarders. The responder might be in an end system or in other equipment, and its distinguishing feature is that it responds to requests at the end of a signalling path. The signalling path traverses an underlying network covering one or more IP hops, which might use locally different technology, so in the quality of service example a forwarder maps service specific information to technology related QoS parameters and receives indications of success or failure. The network can be seen at the level of domains and subdomains rather than individual routers, since domains are assumed to be administrative entities, so security requirements might apply differently between domains and within one.
sections.plainLanguage: Three roles: whoever asks for the service, whoever passes the request along, and whoever answers at the far end. The request normally travels along the same path as the data, but the model also allows a separate signalling path.

sections.title: What Is Assumed and What Is Excluded
sections.content:
The memo states its assumptions. Signalling could run end-to-end, end-to-edge, edge-to-edge or network-to-network between providers, depending on what point in the network acts as the initiator and how far the signalling propagates. In general the memo expects forwarders to become more dense towards the edges of the network, but this is not a requirement: an over-provisioned domain might contain no forwarders at all and be signalling transparent, while at the other extreme forwarders might be placed at every router, in which case QoS provisioning can be carried out locally without further signalling.

Pure end-to-end signalling that is not interpreted anywhere in the network is not considered, since that is a higher layer issue for protocols such as SIP. Where signalling covers several domains, the memo does not exclude different signalling protocols being used in each domain; it only places requirements on the universality of the control information being transported, with the goal of allowing protocols matched to the characteristics of the portion of the network being traversed. The memo also assumes the service definitions an initiator can ask for are known in advance of the signalling protocol running, that there are means for discovering NSIS entities so that signalling peers are known, and that NSIS assumes layer 3 routing, with the determination of the next data node not done by NSIS.

The exclusions are just as long. Development of specific mechanisms and algorithms for application and transport layer adaptation, and the protocols that would support it, are not considered. Specific mechanisms such as APIs for interaction between transport and applications and the network layer are not considered, except to clarify the requirements on negotiation capabilities and information semantics. Specific mechanisms and protocols for provisioning or other network control functions within a domain are not considered, the goal being to reuse existing functions and protocols unchanged, although NSIS itself can be used for signalling within a domain. Interaction with resource management or other internal state management capabilities is not considered. Security implications related to multicasting are outside the scope. Service definitions, and in particular QoS services and classes, are out of scope: only the base signalling protocol for transporting the service information is addressed. Handoff decision and trigger sources are out of scope too: an NSIS protocol is not used to trigger handoffs in mobile IP nor to decide whether to hand off, and the underlying assumption is that the route comes first, defining the path, and the signalling comes after it, following the path.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is careful about what it is not deciding. It does not design a protocol, does not define what a quality of service is, and does not say how a router should hand a phone over to a new base station.

sections.title: The Requirement Groups
sections.content:
Two general and potentially contradictory goals run through the requirements: the solution should be applicable in a very wide range of scenarios, and at the same time be lightweight in implementation complexity and resource consumption in the entities that implement it. One approach is that the solution could deal with certain requirements through modular components or capabilities which are optional to implement or use in individual nodes.

Architecture and design goals: NSIS should provide a mechanism to check whether state is available without setting it up, for example checking resource availability without performing a reservation, which is required in some scenarios such as the mobile terminal case. It must be designed modularly, so that fewer features give lighter implementations, and mutually exclusive solutions are supported, such as working over any kind of network, from narrowband to broadband and from error-prone to reliable. It must decouple the protocol from the information it carries, so the two can develop independently and the control information can be carried within other protocols, including application layer ones, though the information carried still needs to be standardised or interoperability is difficult. It must be independent of the paradigm and mechanism of network control, so that the same signalling can be used with various QoS technologies. It should be able to carry opaque objects interpreted only by some nodes.

Signalling flows: the protocol must work in scenarios such as host-to-network-to-host, edge-to-edge, user-to-network and network-to-network. It must support path-coupled signalling and may support path-decoupled signalling. It should allow the internal structure of a domain to be hidden from end nodes and other networks, for business reasons among others, and it should be possible for signalling for some flows to traverse path segments transparently, without interpretation at the forwarders inside them, as with a subdomain in a core network that only interprets signalling for aggregates established at the domain edge.

Messaging: explicit erasure of state must be possible when state is no longer needed, and state must be released automatically after a failure, to prevent stale state in the network. Notifications should be possible upstream, and both establishment and refusal to set up state must be notified. Local information exchange must be allowed.

Control information: it should be possible to say which parameters may be changed, so that an end-to-end request is not gradually mutated as it passes through nodes. Local scope elements should be added and removed as a message enters and leaves a domain. State must be addressed independently of flow identification, because flows resulting from a handoff may have changed end points but still have the same service requirement. Modification of already established state should be seamless, and grouping the signalling for several micro-flows into one message may be provided, for the optimisation of setup delay, though there must not be any transactional semantic associated with the grouping.

Performance: NSIS must be scalable in the number of messages received by a signalling partner, in the number of hand-offs in mobile environments, in the number of interactions for setting up state, in the amount of state per entity in the core, and in CPU usage on end terminals and intermediate nodes. It must work in Internet scale deployments, and its performance must degrade gracefully rather than catastrophically under overload. It should allow low latency in setup, and must allow low bandwidth consumption, since small sets of scenarios call for it, mainly those where wireless links are involved. It should allow the load on devices to be constrained, through message aggregation, header compression, minimising functionality or ignoring signalling in core nodes.

Flexibility: flow aggregation must be allowed, including the capability to select and change the level of aggregation. Placement of the initiator and responder must be flexible, and network initiated signalling and termination must be allowed in scenarios such as PSTN gateways, some VPNs and mobility. Either the initiator or the responder should be able to initiate a change of state, and the protocol should support network initiated state change, used when the network can no longer guarantee resources and wants to downgrade a reservation. Both unidirectional and bidirectional state setup should be possible, with the goal of bidirectional setup being an optimisation in terms of setup delay.

Mobility: after a handover the states may need to be completely or partially re-established, requested by the mobile node itself or triggered by the access point it is attached to, and the re-establishment must be as quick as possible so that the mobile node does not experience service interruption or degradation. It should be localised and not require end-to-end signalling.

Interworking: the protocol must interwork with IP tunnelling, particularly IPsec tunnels, which mainly affects the identification of flows because parts of the information commonly used for flow identification may not be accessible due to encryption. It must not be constrained to IPv4 or IPv6, and must be independent of the charging model. It should provide hooks for AAA protocols so that usage records can be collected, and should work with seamless handoff protocols such as context transfer and candidate access router discovery. It must work with traditional layer 3 routing, in particular when routes change, so that state on the old route is released and state on the new route is established.

Operational: the architecture should allow the operator to assign signalling messages a certain transport quality, which gives a way to trade off signalling latency against the impact of the messages on devices, and this means the protocol messages should be detectable where their priority is assigned and procedures must be defined for a request that stays unanswered. Any unit participating in signalling must not cause further damage to other systems when it has to go out of service, and entities should be able to detect a malfunctioning peer and notify the initiator or another entity, or handle the problem themselves by switching to a backup entity, in which case state must be synchronised between the primary and the backup.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements fall into ten groups. The short version: the protocol must be modular and cheap, must let the network hide its own shape, must clean up after itself when things fail, must be fast to set up and slow to flood, and must keep working when a phone moves to a different base station.

sections.title: Security Requirements in Detail
sections.content:
The NSIS protocol must provide means for security, but it must be allowed that nodes implementing it do not have to use those means. A signalling protocol must make provision for enabling entities to be authenticated against each other using strong mechanisms, where strong means that weak plain-text password mechanisms must not be used. It must provide means to authorise state setup requests, which demands a hook to interact with a policy entity so that an authenticated entity can be associated with authorisation data and the request verified; authorisation prevents state setup by unauthorised entities, setups that violate policies, and theft of service, and it also limits denial of service attacks caused by unrestricted state setups.

It must provide means to protect message payloads against modification, to prevent an adversary from modifying parts of a signalling message and from mounting denial of service or theft of service attacks against network elements taking part in the exchange. It must provide means to detect old, already transmitted, signalling messages, so that they cannot be replayed, and the solution must cover synchronisation problems in the case of a restart or crash of a participating element.

Channel security between signalling entities must be implemented. It is a well known concept in quality of service and other signalling protocols to have intermediate nodes actively participate in the protocol and modify the messages as required by processing rules. This requirement does not exclude end-to-end or network-to-network security: end-to-end security between the initiator and the responder may be used to protect non-mutable data fields, and network-to-network security refers to protection over various hops but not end to end.

Identity confidentiality should be supported, to enable privacy and avoid profiling of entities by an adversary eavesdropping the signalling traffic, and the identity used in authentication may be hidden to a limited extent from the network the initiator is attached to, though it must provide enough information for the nodes in the access network to collect accounting data. Network topology hiding may be supported, though it might conflict with a diagnostic capability.

Prevention of denial of service attacks should be provided, and to do it effectively the security and protocol mechanisms must have low computational complexity to verify a state setup request before authenticating the requester, and should not require large resource consumption on the entities before a successful authentication is done. Confidentiality of signalling messages in a hop-by-hop manner should be provided, since an adversary who can listen to signalling channels learns which data channels are worth listening to; most messages must be protected hop by hop because the entities taking part in the protocol have to be able to read and eventually modify them. Finally, where existing states have to be modified, a session identifier is needed to identify the established state uniquely, and the protocol must provide security protection to stop adversaries modifying state.
sections.plainLanguage: Signalling messages travel through routers that must read them, so they are protected hop by hop rather than end to end. The rules also insist that checking a request is cheap, so that a flood of signalling cannot be used to overwhelm the network.

sections.title: The Scenarios Behind the Requirements
sections.content:
The appendix holds the use cases the requirements were derived from and tested against. They cover terminal mobility, wireless networks, an example scenario for 3G wireless networks, the wired part of a wireless network, session mobility, and quality of service reservation and negotiation from an access network into a core network and over administrative boundaries.

There are also scenarios for quality of service signalling between PSTN gateways and backbone routers, for a PSTN trunking gateway, for an application that asks the network for an end-to-end quality of service path, and for quality of service in virtual private networks, with the tunnel endpoints at the customer premises and at the provider premises treated separately.
sections.plainLanguage: The scenarios cover a phone moving between base stations, wireless and 3G networks, sessions that follow a user, reservations crossing into a core network and across organisational boundaries, telephone gateways, and quality of service inside VPNs. They are the cases the requirements were checked against.

viz.caption: THE TEN GROUPS THE REQUIREMENTS FALL INTO

cells: Architecture and design goals
Modular design, protocol separated from the information carried, independent of how the network is controlled
Signalling flows
Works wherever the initiator, forwarders and responder sit, path-coupled and optionally path-decoupled
Messaging
State can be erased explicitly and is released automatically after a failure
Control information
Mutability of parameters, local domain information, state addressed apart from the flow
Performance
Scalable, low latency where needed, low bandwidth on wireless links, graceful under overload
Flexibility
Flow aggregation, flexible placement, one or both directions, network initiated changes
Security
Authentication, authorisation, integrity, replay protection, hop-by-hop security, denial of service
Mobility
Service re-established quickly and locally after a handover
Interworking
IP tunnelling, either IP version, charging models, AAA hooks, handoff protocols, ordinary routing
Operational
Transport quality for signalling messages, graceful failure, detection of a faulty peer

viz.caption: THE SECURITY REQUIREMENTS IN ONE PLACE

items.title: Authentication
items.text: Entities authenticate each other with strong mechanisms, never plain-text passwords

items.title: Authorisation
items.text: A policy hook decides who may set up state, which also limits denial of service

items.title: Integrity
items.text: Message payloads are protected against modification

items.title: Replay protection
items.text: Old messages are detected, including after a restart or crash

items.title: Hop-by-hop security
items.text: Each leg is protected, since intermediate nodes must read and change the message

items.title: Denial of service
items.text: Verifying a request before authenticating it must be cheap

items.title: Confidentiality
items.text: Signalling content is hidden hop by hop

items.title: Ownership of state
items.text: A session identifier names the established state, and changes to it are protected
